nameStory: Coralbells gets its charming name from its delicate, bell-shaped flowers that dangle from thin stems like tiny coral-colored chimes. The scientific name 'sanguinea' means 'blood-red,' referring to the deep pink to red blooms that give this plant its coral-like appearance.
description: Coralbells is a compact perennial herb that forms neat clumps of rounded, lobed leaves close to the ground. The plant sends up slender flower stalks topped with airy clusters of small, bell-shaped blooms in shades of deep pink to red. Though native to the American Southwest, it's occasionally found in New England gardens and sometimes escapes cultivation. This low-growing plant typically reaches about 12-18 inches tall when in bloom.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny bell-shaped flowers in deep pink to red colors hang delicately from thin, branching stems. The blooms are sweetly fragrant and feel papery to the touch when dried.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Round to heart-shaped leaves with shallow lobes form a basal rosette close to the ground. The leaves feel somewhat leathery and may have a slightly fuzzy texture on the undersides.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms compact, mounded clumps that stay close to the ground, with flower stems rising well above the foliage. The overall plant has a tidy, cushion-like appearance.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Flower stems are wiry and reddish, feeling smooth but strong. They sway gently in the breeze, making the bell-shaped flowers dance and chime softly together.

habitat: In New England, coralbells is primarily found in cultivated gardens, rock gardens, and perennial borders where it has been planted as an ornamental. It occasionally escapes to naturalize in areas with well-drained, slightly acidic soil. Look for it near old homesteads, abandoned gardens, or in rocky, partially shaded locations.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge fresh and bright green from the crown, and flower buds begin forming on emerging stalks.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season when the sweetly fragrant, bell-shaped flowers are most abundant and attractive to hummingbirds and bees.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade to brown seed heads while leaves may take on reddish tints before going dormant.
seasonality.winter: In milder winters, some leaves may persist close to the ground, appearing bronze or purplish, though most foliage dies back to the crown.

funFact: Coralbells flowers are like a dinner bell for hummingbirds - the birds can actually hear the tiny bells tinkling in the breeze and associate that sound with a nectar reward, making gardens with coralbells into musical hummingbird magnets!
confusionNotes: Coralbells might be confused with wild ginger due to its heart-shaped basal leaves, but wild ginger has much larger, broader leaves and lacks the distinctive airy flower clusters. Remember: if you see tiny dancing bells above the leaves, it's coralbells!
contextualKnowledge: Though called coralbells, this plant is not related to coral at all - it's a member of the saxifrage family, which means 'rock-breaker.' Many gardeners know various colorful-leaved cultivars as 'heuchera,' using the scientific genus name, but the original wild species has the classic green foliage.
compareHints: Coralbells differs from its relative American alumroot by having much showier, more colorful flowers in deep pink to red rather than the greenish-white blooms of American alumroot. Coralbells also has a more compact growth habit and more distinctly bell-shaped flowers, while American alumroot tends to be taller with smaller, less noticeable blooms.

relatedSpecies.distinction: American alumroot differs from its garden cousin coralbells by having more subdued coloring and smaller, less showy flowers.
